title: Prime positive-cone ideals and convex subgroups
statement:
Let $\Gamma$ be a totally ordered abelian group [def-trf-totally-ordered-abelian-group]. An ideal is an upward-closed subset $I\subseteq\Gamma_{\ge0}$, and it is prime when $0
otin I$ and $\gamma+\delta\in I$ for nonnegative $\gamma,\delta$ implies $\gamma\in I$ or $\delta\in I$. Then prime ideals of this positive cone, ordered by inclusion, are canonically order anti-isomorphic to convex subgroups of $\Gamma$, ordered by inclusion (a subgroup $H$ is convex when $h_1,h_2\in H$ and $h_1\le x\le h_2$ imply $x\in H$): a convex subgroup $H$ corresponds to $I_H=\{\gamma\in\Gamma_{\ge0}:\gamma
otin H\}$, and a prime ideal $I$ corresponds to $H_I=\{\gamma\in\Gamma:|\gamma|
otin I\}$, where $|\gamma|$ is the larger of $\gamma$ and $-\gamma$.

proof.text: Order calculations used below. By [def-trf-totally-ordered-abelian-group], translating $a\le b$ by $-a-b$ gives $-b\le-a$. Totality gives $|x|=x$ if $x\ge0$, and $|x|=-x$ if $x\le0$; hence $|x|\ge0$, $|0|=0$, $|-x|=|x|$, and $-|x|\le x\le|x|$. Adding the two upper bounds for $x,y$ gives $x+y\le|x|+|y|$, while adding the bounds for $-x,-y$ gives $-(x+y)\le|x|+|y|$. Whichever of $x+y$ and $-(x+y)$ is larger therefore satisfies $|x+y|\le|x|+|y|$.

proof.text: Let $I$ be prime and set $S=\Gamma_{\ge0}\setminus I$. Then $0\in S$. If $s\in S$ and $0\le t\le s$, then $t\in I$ would force $s\in I$ by upward closure, so $t\in S$. If $s,t\in S$, then $s+t\ge0$ by translation invariance [def-trf-totally-ordered-abelian-group]; if $s+t\in I$, primality would force $s\in I$ or $t\in I$. Hence $S$ is downward closed in $\Gamma_{\ge0}$ and closed under addition.

source.place: Tag 00IE, definition-value-group, and the preceding definition of a totally ordered abelian group; elementary argument from the displayed formulas, not a quoted Stacks correspondence theorem.

proof.text: Put $H_I=\{x:|x|\in S\}$, which is exactly the set in the statement. By Steps 1 and 3, $0\in H_I$, and $x\in H_I$ implies $-x\in H_I$. If $x,y\in H_I$, Step 3 gives $|x|+|y|\in S$; Step 1 and downward closure then give $|x+y|\in S$. Thus $x+y\in H_I$, so $H_I$ is a subgroup. These are precisely the subgroup axioms inside the abelian group of [def-trf-totally-ordered-abelian-group].

proof.text: To check convexity, let $a,b\in H_I$ and $a\le x\le b$. If $x\ge0$, then $|x|=x$ and $0\le x\le b\le|b|$; since $|b|\in S$, downward closure gives $|x|\in S$. If $x\le0$, reversing $a\le x$ gives $0\le-x\le-a\le|a|$; since $|a|\in S$ and $|x|=-x$, again $|x|\in S$. Totality [def-trf-totally-ordered-abelian-group] supplies one of these two cases, so $x\in H_I$.

proof.text: For a subgroup $H$ and any $x$, $|x|\in H$ if and only if $x\in H$: by totality $|x|$ is either $x$ or $-x$, and a subgroup is closed under negation [def-trf-totally-ordered-abelian-group]. Thus $x\in H_{I_H}$ if and only if $|x|\notin I_H$, if and only if $|x|\in H$, if and only if $x\in H$. For $a\ge0$, $|a|=a$, so $a\in I_{H_I}$ if and only if $a\notin H_I$, if and only if $a\in I$. These pointwise equalities prove that the two constructions are inverse.
